title: The Golden Deer
hook: a golden deer and a cry in Rama's voice: Nyaya's name for a reason that only looks like one
carry: hetvabhasa: a reason that only looks real
tomorrow: a boy at Death's door is offered every treasure. what does he want instead?

segments.voice: Yesterday, King Janaka's debate: Gargi asked to find out, Shakalya pushed to win, and Nyaya calls them vada and jalpa.

In the forest at Panchavati, Sita sees a deer at the edge of the clearing, and it doesn't look like any deer. Its coat is gold, flecked with silver, and it glows. She asks Rama to catch it for her. Lakshmana, Rama's brother, frowns. No deer like that exists, he says. That's a demon in disguise. He's right. It's Maricha, sent by Ravana: a shape-shifter wearing a shape too beautiful to resist. Rama goes after it anyway, and leaves Lakshmana to guard Sita.
screen: `A DEER MADE OF GOLD.` → `NO DEER LOOKS LIKE THAT.` → `IT'S MARICHA, IN DISGUISE.`

segments.voice: Deep in the forest, Rama's arrow finds the deer. And as Maricha dies, he does one last thing. He cries out in Rama's own voice: oh Sita, oh Lakshmana. Back at the hut, Sita hears it. That's Rama, she thinks, so Rama is in danger. Go! Lakshmana says nothing can harm his brother. She won't hear it, she speaks to him harshly, and he goes. With the hut unguarded, Ravana steps out of the trees. That's the Ramayana, and it turns on two things that only looked real: a deer that shone like gold, and a voice that sounded exactly like Rama. Nyaya has a name for the second kind of trap: hetvabhasa. Hetu is a reason; abhasa is a semblance, something that shines like what it isn't. The Nyaya Sutra lists five. The first is the wandering reason: a sign that shows up where your conclusion is true, and also where it isn't. Rama's voice crying out shows up when Rama is in danger. It also shows up when a shape-shifter copies him. So it can't settle anything. Nyaya didn't write about Sita; that's a reading, through its list. But notice who gets fooled: not a careless person, Sita herself. That's why Nyaya takes this seriously. Its Sutra opens by tying freedom from false knowledge to the highest good. For this school, checking a reason is spiritual work, because false knowledge is where suffering gets in. Today the voices come by text. Before you run, ask the Nyaya question: does this sign also show up when nothing's wrong?
screen: `A VOICE THAT SOUNDS LIKE RAMA.` · `HETVABHASA: A LOOK-ALIKE REASON.` · `THE WANDERING REASON.` · `EVEN SITA WAS FOOLED.` · then, large: `DOES IT SHOW UP WHEN NOTHING'S WRONG?`

segments.voice: Sit with the breath, and bring to mind one because you've believed lately, about someone or about yourself. Say the reason quietly and ask: does this sign also show up when it isn't true? Don't argue with it; just look. If you pray, there's an old prayer for exactly this, from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad: asato ma sad gamaya, lead me from the unreal to the real. If you don't pray, say: let me see what's really there.
Nyaya. Today, hetvabhasa: a reason that only looks like a reason, like a cry that sounds just like Rama.
Your line: hetvabhasa, a reason that only looks real. Even Sita heard the false voice. Go gently.

fork.setup: you hear a cry in a voice exactly like Rama's. by Nyaya, what's wrong with "that's his voice, so he's in danger"?
options: nothing: a voice you know is proof enough.
the reason wanders: that voice also shows up when a shape-shifter copies him.
the reason flips: hearing him proves he's safe.
fork.reveal: a wandering reason shows up where the conclusion is false too. Maricha could copy the voice, so the voice alone couldn't settle it.

original.note: Sanskrit: hetvabhasa, from hetu, a reason, and abhasa, a semblance: a false reason.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bad argument is just a wrong one.
what it means: some reasons only shine like reasons. Nyaya names them, and treats seeing through them as part of the path, since false knowledge is where suffering gets in.

what a scholar hears: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Maricha's deer and the false cry); Nyaya Sutra 1.2.4–9 lists five hetvabhasas, first savyabhichara, the wandering reason; 1.1.2 ties removing false knowledge to release.

chat.meaning: A wandering reason shows up whether the conclusion is true or not. Maricha's cry sounded like Rama in danger, and it wasn't. Nyaya calls reasons like that hetvabhasa.
